sections.content: The course covers basic psychology concepts across around 12 topics, including research methods, neuroscience, sensation and perception, consciousness, memory, learning, development, stress and health, social psychology, individual differences, psychological disorders, and treatment. The content is broad rather than deep, so it is generally manageable. If you have some background in biology, the terminology will not be difficult to memorize. Overall, the course serves as a straightforward introduction to psychology.
sections.teaching: The instructor is very kind and patient. Lectures are clear, direct, and well-structured, and classes usually end on time. Although there is a slight accent, it does not significantly affect comprehension. Most of the teaching content follows the lecture slides closely, which makes the material easy to follow and revise.
sections.grading:
The workload is relatively light. There is one essay, two exams, in-class activities, and a research participation component. The essay can be completed within a few days, and both the midterm and final exams require limited preparation time since the content is not extensive and exams are multiple-choice only. Overall, the time investment is low compared to the return.

Overall:
A well-structured and beginner-friendly psychology course with light workload and fair grading. Suitable for students looking for an introductory course with relatively low stress.
sections.workload: The grading scheme is clear and transparent: in-class activities (10%), research experience (5%), essay (25%), midterm (30%), and final (30%). In-class activities and research experience are easy to score full marks as long as you participate. Exams are straightforward but competitive, as the overall average is high, leaving little room for careless mistakes. Grading is fair, but students need to be accurate to secure a top grade.

Psychological Research Methods
Sensation and Perception (How our brains process visual cues)
Circadian Rhythm and Sleep (The science behind sleep cycles)
Consciousness (Implicit and explicit information processing, featuring everyone's favorite Freud)

Learning (Conditioning and Observational Learning)
Memory (Long- and short-term memory; memorization strategies)

Motivation (Theories explaining motivation; Hierarchy of needs)

sections.teaching:
Kevin taught well. He elaborated on the concepts presented in the PPTs by either playing supplementary videos, doing small-scale experiments with us, or providing us with more examples. He had a slight Hong Kong accent which did not impede our understanding.

The teaching team was receptive of questions in general - Kevin would gladly answer your questions during the break or after the lessons, and that served to help me clear up the definitions of some of the concepts which were quite similar. Both the TA and Kevin responded to questions about course assignments clearly.

The workshop run by the TA taught us research skills for us to do the essay such as finding sources and citing them in APA, which were helpful if this is your first essay course but not useful otherwise.
sections.grading:
The grading scheme was reasonable, but the grading was quite competitive.

Grading Scheme:
Workshop Worksheet (5%)*
Research Experience (5%)*
Learning Reflection (5%)*
Essay (15%)
Midterm Exam (30%)
Final Exam (40%)

The components marked with an asterisk (*) were graded on a pass-fail basis. This means that you either get all of the points or none of them. For failed pass-fail components, you can resubmit with a 50% penalty to the score.

You can choose to attend a real research study in HKUST, or watch a video about a classic study and submit a reflection report (~250 words) for the research experience part.

The workshop worksheet was preparation for the essay as it gave you the opportunity to practice finding and evaluating sources.

The learning reflection was a ~250 word piece for you to "reflect on what has been taught in the course", which should not be too difficult if you had been listening to the lectures.

Both the final and the midterm were MCQs. Each MCQ represents one final mark, but they were not difficult at all. This led to a pretty high mean, and careless mistakes can kill you pretty quickly.

Research Experience: 0/5/4.87/5/5/5/5

Getting 90 resulted in an A, which was slightly disappointing but acceptable.
sections.workload:
Workload was quite low throughout the course.

Attending the lectures were fun but not really necessary. The workshops were useful if you have not written an essay before; not very useful otherwise.

Both the workshop worksheet and the learning reflection took less than 2-3 hours to write, and shouldn't be a huge burden on your time.

The main workload of the essay comes from finding all the sources you need and integrating them to form a coherent argument. The number of sources is less important than the quality and your interpretation - don't spend your time finding 20+ sources which can't help you, and focus on forming a coherent point with less sources.

The midterm and finals were MCQs based on different scenarios. Although it still involved a fair amount of rote memorization, it was way less painful to revise for than some other courses (cough cough PHYS 1001). Understanding the concepts would help you much more than reciting verbatim. (Maybe use the memorization strategies taught?)

The most annoying part was registering for the research experience component and actually remembering to show up. Remember to register early since each timeslot didn't have a lot of vacancies.

sections.workload:
Preparing for the quizzes is not difficult. Going through all the lecture slides and extra slides (provided during lectures) is enough. Note that a few questions in the quizzes are based on the extra slides (Don't skip lectures if you want to score high!). Most of the questions are conceptual, i.e. testing whether you can understand the concepts / distinguish between different concepts. Not much memorization of details is required. If you understand all the concepts clearly, you will be fine.

Tips: Each MCQ consists of 4 options. You may anticipate that questions with a set of 4 similar concepts as the 4 options will more likely to appear in the quizzes. Here is an example (created by me):

(#07 Learning) Taking away a child's favorite toy as the result of his misbehavior at school is an example of ...
A. positive reinforcement
B. negative reinforcement
C. positive punishment
*D. negative punishment

I think the workload mainly comes from the essay. The topic of the essay was announced a few days after the add/drop period, and the deadline for the essay was set during the midterm period (Week 8). You have more than 1 month to complete the essay. The essay will probably clash with your midterm(s) if you are a deadline fighter.

sections.workload:
Heavy workload if you don't like writing, but otherwise it's gonna be a piece of cake for you.

It requires you to submit an 800-word essay addressing several questions or issues raised by an essay prompt. Integration of concepts from different lectures is required and you definitely have to spend much time on it. Sometimes the situation is quite ambiguous and you might have to burn your brain to make sure EVERY concept in the essay is correctly applied. If any wrong concept appears, your essay will definitely score VERY low. The word limit cannot be exceeded or otherwise marks deducted, and you'll have to address all the questions thoroughly with concrete examples, evidence and some research within the word limit. I spent so much time in cutting the number of words and it was a nightmare. But at the end the essay turned out to be the savior of my grade.

In addition to the essays, there are a total of three exams. Though they are all MC questions, it doesn't mean the exams are easy. I spent several weeks on revising the lecture ppts but still did not get a very good result in the exams.

As a tip of ur revision, cuz all exams are in MCs, there is no need for u to completely memorize all those fancy terms and names. All u need to do is to recognize the first 3 alphabetical letters of each name and as soon as u can recognize and differentiate different concepts, and u understand wut they are, then u're done. It all tests ur ability to RECOGNIZE but not RECALL.

Another component of the course is research participation which accounts for 10% of the course grade. It was the worst sh!t of my life cuz it was really hard to enroll in one. After I received the research email I immediately rushed to the SONA website to register, but still... DAMN!!! "Timeslot is already full..." You can never imagine why all the other people can grab all the places sooooo FAST!!!

sections.content: Topics covered in this course: Research Methods, Memory, Learning, Development, Sensation and Perception, States of Consciousness, Intelligence, Personality, Social Psychology, Psychological Disorders, Treatment of Psychological Disorders and Health & Well-being. Most of the PowerPoints are short (about 20-40 pages each) and consist of key concepts only which are easy to understand. Some of the contents are quite interesting, such as the experiments, for example, the Bobo Doll experiment, that were carried out to investigate certain theories related to psychology.
sections.teaching: The instructor teaches in a fun way, she is very nice and always smiles when she talks and tries to make the atmosphere very relaxing. You won't fall asleep easily in this class. Also, there are musical warmups in the first 5 minutes of class, a small break halfway through the lecture, and often video clips about some experiments or studies will be shown. Sometimes she will ask students questions about their opinions/thoughts on a topic, and she will give interesting responses.
sections.grading:
Grading is as follows:
25% + 25% Mid-Term Exam + Final Exam
20% + 20% Paper Assignment 1 & 2
10% Research Participation
1% + 1% Bonus (Writing Workshop + Guest Lecture)
No taking of attendance required.

Both exams consist of fully MC questions. If you understand the concepts well enough, you can easily score high in both exams. No need to memorize large amounts of points/notes/materials.

Paper assignments are the most difficult part of this course. You need to write an essay of no more than 500 words about a specific topic/issue. Essays need to follow the APA citation format, which is discussed during the writing workshop. Proper citation is required as plagiarism will be checked during marking.

Research participation requires you to take 3 surveys. You need to apply through the SONA system yourself. If you complete all 3 surveys, you can get all 10% of this part, which is easy to achieve.

Finally, there are 2 opportunities for bonus points, one is the writing workshop, and the other is a guest lecture by a counselor.
My results are: above 1 SD in both exams, above 0.5 SD in essay 1, mean in essay 2, final grade is A. Grading is very good in my opinion.
sections.workload: Workload is light, only 2 paper assignments and 2 exams in the whole term. For exams, you only need to study the PPTs, there is no need to study the textbook (although it is recommended). Research participation is easy and only take a max of 1.5 hours in total (just register ASAP for the surveys). Full attendance of lectures is not required, although attending will certainly help you familiarize with the concepts.
